newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE - Malaysia rainforest beckons electronics firms.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Malaysia rainforest beckons electronics firms.

text.p: Malaysia's sparsely-populated, rainforest state of Sarawak, with its rich history of white Rajahs and headhunters, is beckoning high-technology industries.

Sarawak, as large as penisular Malaysia itself and best known outside the region as an exporter of tropical timber, is setting up an industrial park for electronics companies and a zone on the information technology superhighway.
Sarawak is wooing multinationals and training residents for jobs created by huge infrastructure projects and a nearly decade-long economic boom.
In jungles where tribesmen still hunt birds and boar with blowpipes, huge projects like the 15 billion ringgit ($5.5 billion) Bakun hydo-electric dam are taking shape.

The controversial dam -- it will create a reservoir as large as Singapore, displace nearly 10,000 tribespeople and clear 69,000 hectares (170,502 acres) of forest -- has been slammed by critics worried about its environmental impact.
But Sarawak officials say it will be the catalyst for downstream industries and provide stable employment for longhouse dwellers who still live mostly by barter.

Other projects are concentrated mainly in the eastern town of Bintulu, including a 20 billion ringgit ($8.1 billion) industrial park, a two billion ringgit paper and pulp factory, and a two billion ringgit aluminium smelting plant.
Sarawak is targeting average economic growth of 10 percent a year between 1996 and 2000.
MALAYSIA'S SILICON VALLEY
Sarawak is aiming to attract electronics firms in northern Penang state, Malaysia's "Silicon Valley", to expand their operations in Sarawak.

The national carrier Malaysia Airline System Bhd last month introduced twice weekly flights betwen Penang and Kuching city mainly to accommodate the electronics industry, said K. Gopalan, a manager at the Penang Development Corporation.
"Basically, the volume is there," he told Reuters.
Sarawak is promoting itself as part of the East Asia Growth Area, an evolving free trade zone encompassing the rest of Borneo, southern Philippines and Indonesia's Sulawesi island.

Sarawak also plans to set up an area for investment by world-class information technology companies along the lines of Peninsular Malaysia's Multimedia Super Corridor, said Sarawak's Industrial Development Minister Abang Johari Abang Openg.
LABOUR CONCERNS
"We are going for high-tech automation...where you don't need a lot of labour. That is, the upper end of industry," Abang Johari told Reuters.
But a major concern is the possibility Sarawak will soon face a shortage of workers needed to carry out the big projects and the skilled professionals to lead them.
It has already had to import hundreds of thousands of workers, mainly from neighbouring Kalimantan -- the Indonesian province on Borneo -- many of whom are working illegally, officials say.

The state's gross domestic product (GDP) notched an average annual growth rate of 7.3 percent between 1990 and 1995, including 13.5 percent in 1995. This compares with Malaysian GDP growth of 9.5 percent in 1995.
ECONOMY RESTRUCTURED
Sarawak Chief Minister Abdul Taib Mahmud said recently the economy has been restructured in the last 15 years.
"Right from the early 1980s we have been able to slowly shift from our traditional sector to the manufacturing sector," he told a business conference in the state capital, Kuching.

Most of Sarawak's 24 ethnic groups have since been brought into the mainstream of development. Of the 1.84 million residents, about 30 percent each are Ibans and Chinese. Malays, Melanau, Bidayuhs and Orang Ulus form large minority races.
Sarawak, a British colony between 1946 and 1963, joined the Malaysia Federation in 1963, along with Malaysia's Sabah state and Singapore. Singapore was expelled two years later.

Abdul Taib said 65 percent of Sarawak's labour force today is involved in "modern" economic activities, compared with 1980 when 60 percent were doing "traditional" activities -- slash and burn agriculture, hunting and gathering.
Manufacturing is now the key growth sector, contributing 20.4 percent to Sarawak's gross domestic product (GDP) from only 6.5 percent in 1981, when Taib became chief minister.
The sector includes petroleum and petrochemical products, downstream wood-processing, commercial agriculture-based industries and the high-technology sector.
Sarawak-based industrialist, Philip Ting, while very bullish about economic prospects in the state, said he was concerned about the labour force.
"We are reaching full employment and skilled people are needed. We need to attract skilled people and technology," the group managing director of Cahya Mata Sarawak Bhd told a business conference.
PRESERVING VALUES
"Sarawak cannot go into labour-intensive business. Sarawak can't afford to have three people trying to fix a door," Zawawi Ismail, vice-chancellor at University Malaysia Sarawak told Reuters.
As Sarawak moves into the information age, officials say the older way of life has to be left behind, though like other developing Asian nations, it wants to retain its proud traditions.

"The romantic notion of preserving the older way of life, I think is no longer valid. Every Sarawakian has an equal right to progress," Zawawi said. "What is important is the preserving of values and culture." ($1 = 2.4800 ringgit)
